Q. 
Please explain how the Company developed its base delivery revenue 
5 
forecast for the Rate Year. 
6 
A. 
For firm sales and transportation service classifications (SC 1, 2, 3, 9, 15, 
7 
16 and 17), the base delivery revenue forecast was developed based on the 
8 
forecast number of customers and deliveries.  Deliveries were allocated to 
9 
the usage blocks within each service class using an ogive analysis, which 
10 
uses historic bill frequencies to develop a cumulative percentage 
11 
distribution for usage levels within a service class.  This cumulative 
12 
distribution is then used to allocate the forecast deliveries into the usage 
13 
blocks for each service class, after which the deliveries can be priced at the 
14 
applicable rate for the particular block.   
15 
 
16 
As discussed in detail below, the Company is proposing new service 
17 
classifications (SC 18 and 19) that blends all TC and IT customers (current 
18 
SC 4, 7, 12, and 13).  The revenue forecast for the new non-firm demand 
19 
response class under SC 18 and 19was not based on an ogive analysis 
20 
because the rate structure consists of a customer charge and a single 
21 
11


--- Page 12 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 10 of 74 
 
volumetric block.  The revenue forecasts for SC 4, 7, 12, and 13 were used 
1 
to develop rates for SC 18 and 19. 
2 
 
3 
Q. 
How were the remaining revenue forecast components developed, 
4 
specifically for the MFC, SBC, CEF, EES, and TRS? 
5 
A. 
These additional revenue components are separate surcharges that are 
6 
applied to specific service classes as described in the Tariff.  To develop the 
7 
revenue forecast for these components, the Company applied specific 
8 
unitized rates to appropriate service class delivery volumes.  The MFC 
9 
surcharge, which is designed to recover gas supply-related costs, was 
10 
developed based on the New York Mercantile Exchange (“NYMEX”) 
11 
forward gas prices as of December 26, 2018.   
12 
 
13 
 
The SBC, consisting of the CEF and EES (also referred to as the Efficiency 
14

the costs associated with the Company’s New York State Energy Research 
16 
and Development Authority (“NYSERDA”) and energy efficiency program 
17

18 
based on a projection of the Company’s energy efficiency program

V. 
Embedded Cost of Service Study 
7 
A. Purpose of ECOSS and Overview of Methodology 
8 
Q. 
What is an ECOSS and what is its purpose? 
9 
A. 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion a utility’s total revenue 
10 
requirement, including plant and other investments, operating expenses, 
11 
depreciation, and taxes among the rate classes served by the utility.  The 
12 
ECOSS computes, for each class, the revenue that must be collected from 
13 
that class to produce the system average rate of return on rate base.  This 
14 
information provides guidance in revenue allocation and in the development 
15 
of rates. 
16 
 
17 
Q. 
Please summarize the methodology employed for the ECOSS. 
18 
A. 
The ECOSS is prepared by analyzing each element of the utility’s revenue 
19 
requirement and assigning or allocating it among the rate classes.  The 
20 
ECOSS was performed using a specialized model developed by HSG 
21 
15


--- Page 16 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 14 of 74 
 
Group.  This model uses the traditional three-step process as follows: 
1 
• Functionalization – Each of the Company’s costs and expenses, as 
2 
well as rate base components, are assigned or allocated among each 
3 
of the gas functions identified in Appendix A to the Commission’s 
4 
November 9, 2001 Order in Case 00-M-0504. 
5 
• Classification – Each functionalized cost element is separated into 
6 
demand, commodity, and customer cost categories. 
7 
• Class allocation – Each functionally classified cost element is 
8 
assigned or allocated among one or more of the Company’s rate 
9 
classes. 
10 
 
11 
Q. 
Please describe the functionalization step of the ECOSS. 
12 
A. 
In the functionalization step, cost elements are separated among the utility’s 
13 
basic service functions by determining what physical purpose each cost 
14 
element serves. 
15 
 
16 
Q. 
What are the functions included in the ECOSS? 
17 
A. 
The functions included in the ECOSS are: 
18 
• Supply and Storage – availability and supply of gas and storage to 
19 
meet seasonal and daily peak demands; 
20 
• Transmission – moves gas from supply and storage sources to 
21 
16


--- Page 17 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 15 of 74 
 
localized distribution facilities; 
1 
• Distribution – moves gas from the transmission system to 
2 
customers’ premises (includes service lines); 
3 
• Metering and Billing – connects customers to the system, measures 
4 
their usage and demand, and bills for the services provided; 
5 
• Collections;  
6 
• Sales Promotion; and  
7 
• Procurement. 
8 
 
9 
Q. 
Please describe the classification step of the ECOSS. 
10 
A. 
The Company’s gas distribution system is designed to meet three primary 
11 
objectives: 
12 
1. Connect customers to the Company’s distribution system; 
13 
2. Meet the aggregate peak design day capacity requirements of all 
14 
customers entitled to service on the peak day; and 
15 
3. Deliver natural gas commodity to customers, whether they are sales 
16 
or transportation customers. 
17 
 
Based on these objectives, each functionalized cost element is classified as 
18 
being customer-related, demand-related, or commodity-related, depending 
19 
on which of the foregoing objectives it serves. 
20 
 
21 
17


--- Page 18 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 16 of 74 
 
 
Cost elements classified as customer-related are incurred to attach a 
1 
customer to the distribution system, meter gas usage, and maintain the 
2 
customer’s account.  Customer-related cost elements are primarily a 
3 
function of the number of customers served and are incurred by the 
4 
Company whether or not an individual customer uses any gas.  Such costs 
5 
may include capital costs associated with the customer component of 
6 
distribution mains, as well as costs for services, meters and metering, 
7 
billing, customer service, and accounting and collection activities. 
8 
 
9 
 
Demand or capacity related cost elements are associated with plant that is 
10 
designed, installed, and operated to meet peak hourly or daily customer gas 
11 
flow requirements.  Demand-related components include transmission and 
12 
distribution mains, localized distribution facilities, and dedicated facilities 
13 
that are designed to satisfy individual customer maximum demands.  
14 
Demand-related cost elements are allocated among the classes based on 
15 
their contributions to the peak demand for which the system is designed. 
16 
 
17 
 
Cost elements classified as commodity-related generally vary with the 
18 
volume of gas sold or delivered (i.e., throughput) to customers.  Costs 
19 
related to obtaining gas supply are classified as commodity-related. 
20 
 
21 
18


--- Page 19 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 17 of 74 
 
Q. 
How were costs functionalized to Supply-Storage classified? 
1 
A. 
The classification step for Supply-Storage separated those costs into costs 
2 
recovered through the GAC, and other costs related to supply and storage.  
3 
The amount of costs recovered through the GAC was equal to the GAC 
4 
revenue. 
5 
 
6 
Q. 
Please describe the process for determining how much of the 
7 
investment in mains should be considered customer-related versus 
8 
demand-related. 
9 
A. 
Distribution mains are installed to connect customers to the distribution 
10 
system (customer-related) as well as to provide capacity to meet customer 
11 
requirements on the design day (demand-related).  Therefore, the cost of 
12 
mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly demand-related.  
13 
Based on the results of its minimum-system study, the Company estimated 
14 
the customer component of mains to be 46.17 percent and the demand 
15 
component 53.83 percent.  The customer component was allocated among 
16 
the customer classes based on the number of customers.  The demand 
17 
component was allocated among the customer classes based on their 
18 
contribution to design-day demand. 
19 
 
20 
Q. 
Please describe how the minimum-system study was performed. 
21 
19


--- Page 20 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 18 of 74 
 
A. 
Minimum-system studies are a widely accepted method to classify mains 
1 
between customer- and demand-related costs.  The customer-related 
2 
component is the portion of cost representing the least-cost system the 
3 
utility would install simply to connect customers, without regard to the need 
4 
to meet demand. 
5 
 
6 
The analysis begins by obtaining from plant and accounting records the cost 
7 
of mains the utility has installed in recent years, detailed by material 
8 
(plastic, steel, and cast iron), length, and diameter.  Then the installed cost 
9 
per foot is computed for each material / diameter type. 
10 
 
11 
The minimum system ratio is computed as the ratio of (X), the cost of 
12 
replacing the entire mains distribution system with the minimum 
13 
component, which is two-inch plastic, to (Y), the cost of replacing the entire 
14 
mains distribution system with plastic of the same diameter as-installed. 
15 
 
16 
This produced a minimum system ratio of 46.17 percent, which represents 
17 
the portion of total mains cost simply to connect customers without regard 
18 
to meeting their design-day demands (i.e., customer-related costs). 
19 
 
20 
Q. 
Please explain the allocation step of the ECOSS. 
21 
20


--- Page 21 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 19 of 74 
 
A. 
In the allocation phase of the ECOSS, the cost elements that have been 
1 
functionalized and classified are allocated among the service classes.  There 
2 
are two types of allocation factors, or allocators, that are used for this 
3 
purpose: external allocators and internal allocators.  External allocators are 
4 
based on special studies derived from data in the Company’s accounting 
5 
and other records.  For example, the number of customers by service class 
6 
is an external allocator that was used in the Company’s ECOSS to allocate 
7 
some of the customer care costs.  Other examples of external allocators 
8 
include annual deliveries, design day requirements, and historic bad debt 
9 
experience.  Internal allocators are based on some combination of external 
10 
allocators, costs that are directly assigned, and other internal allocators.  For 
11 
example, the allocator for property insurance expense is based on plant 
12 
investment assigned to each service class; therefore, it is necessary to 
13 
compute plant investment by service class before property insurance costs 
14 
can be allocated among the classes. 
15

A. 
In developing the Company’s proposed revenue allocation, the Panel 
1

2

13

VII. 
Lost and Unaccounted for Gas   
3 
Q. 
Is the Company updating its LAUF target? 
4 
A. 
Yes.  As shown on Exhibit ___ (RDP-5), the Company updated its LAUF 
5 
target to reflect the experience of the last five GAC years (twelve-month 
6 
periods ended August 31, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, and 2018) using the 
7 
methodology adopted in the 2016 KEDLI Rate Case.  This is also consistent 
8 
with the LAUF White Paper published by the Department of Public Service 
9 
Staff in Case 12-G-0544.  The updated LAUF target is 3.218 percent with a 
10 
standard deviation of 1.166 percent.  The dead band is equal to 2 standard 
11 
deviations from the LAUF target and has an upper band of 5.550 percent 
12 
and lower band of .886 percent.  The Company will reconcile its 
13 
performance under the LAUF incentive as part of its annual Gas Cost 
14 
Reconciliation filing.  
15 
 
16 
Q. 
Is the Company proposing any changes to the current LAUF 
17 
mechanism? 
18 
A. 
Yes.    First, the Company is proposing to discontinue the inactive account 
19 
adjustment beginning on September 1, 2020.  Second, the Company is 
20 
proposing to implement the updated LAUF targets effective September 1, 
21 
37


--- Page 38 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 36 of 74 
 
2020.  Third, the Company is changing its factor of adjustment calculation. 
1 
 
2 
 Q. 
Why is the Company proposing to remove the inactive account 
3 
adjustment? 
4 
A. 
In accordance with the Joint Proposal in the 2016 KEDLI Rate Case, 
5 
beginning on September 1, 2017, the Company adjusted the annual LAUF 
6 
calculation for an estimate of gas usage associated with inactive meters.  
7 
However, the adjustment for inactive accounts double counts the impacts of 
8 
inactive accounts in the LAUF calculation.  Because an inactive account is 
9 
an account that has gas flowing without a customer of record, it would not 
10 
be included in metered deliveries when the Company calculates the actual 
11 
LAUF.  Therefore, inactive account usage is already increasing the 
12 
Company’s losses, and to the extent that actual LAUF is above the upper 
13 
deadband, the Company incurs a penalty for inactive account usage.  For 
14 
this reason, the Company believes the requirement to adjust actual LAUF 
15 
for inactive account usage is unnecessary.   
16 
 
17

X. 
Revenue Decoupling Mechanism  
2 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s current RDM. 
3 
A. 
Under the Company’s current RDM, a revenue per customer target is set for 
4 
delivery service revenues from customers taking service under SC 1B – 
5 
Residential Heating, and actual revenues are trued up against the revenue 
6 
per customer target annually.  For SC 2 and SC 3 customers, a revenue per 
7 
class target is set for delivery service revenues from those customers and 
8 
actual revenues are trued up against those revenue per class targets annually.  
9 
Any over/under collections from the SC 3 class are refunded or collected 
10 
from all SC 3 customers in the following year.  Any over/under collections 
11 
for SC 2 heat and SC 2 non-heat customers are aggregated and collected 
12 
from or refunded to all SC 2 customers in the following year.  In addition, 
13 
any customer growth that exceeds the growth assumed in the revenue 
14 
forecast is calculated at a marginal cost rate and is an adjustment to the 
15 
annual RDM reconciliation.  The annual average number of customers 
16 
included in the sales forecast for the SC 2 heat, SC 2 non-heat, and SC 3 
17 
classes is compared to the actual annual average number of customers in the 
18 
reconciliation year.  This comparison excludes any customer migration that 
19 
occurs in the Rate Year between the SC 2 non-heat and SC 2 heat classes.  
20 
After making the adjustment for SC 2 customer migration, if the actual 
21 
47


--- Page 48 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI)

annual average number of customers is greater than the forecast annual 
1 
average number of customers, the difference is multiplied by the marginal 
2 
cost rates established in the MCS and removed from the actual revenues 
3 
used to calculate the RDM over or under collection for the applicable rate 
4 
year.  In addition, revenues obtained from TC and IT customers that migrate 
5 
to SC 2 and SC 3 firm service classes are excluded.

XIII. 
Commitments from 2016 KEDLI Rate Case 
18 
A. Inclining Block Study 
19 
Q. 
Has the Company performed an inclining block study as required in 
20 
the 2016 KEDLI Rate Case? 
21 
70


--- Page 71 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 69 of 74 
 
A. 
Yes.  Pursuant to the “Order Adopting Terms of Joint Proposal and 
1 
Establishing Gas Rate Plans” in the 2016 KEDLI Rate Case, the Company 
2 
examined the effects of modifying the current residential rate design, which 
3 
is a fixed monthly charge with declining block rates.  The Company 
4 
examined four block designs: (i) the rate design proposed herein, which 
5 
maintains the present ratio of tail block rate to mid-block rate (24 percent 
6 
for SC 1A and 23 percent for SC 1B; (ii) reducing the slope (i.e., increasing 
7 
the ratio of tail block to mid-block) by 50 percent; (iii) flat rates (i.e., tail 
8 
block equals mid blocks, eliminating the blocked structure); and (iv) 
9 
inclining blocks where the tail block is 125 percent of the mid-block.  The 
10 
results of the study are shown in Exhibit ___ (RDP-11), Schedule 1. 
11 
 
12 
Q. 
Please summarize the results of the study. 
13 
A. 
Exhibit ___ (RDP-11) shows that as declining block rates are eliminated 
14 
and the rate design moves toward inclining block rates, the changes in 
15 
delivery revenue from current rates becomes more pronounced.  For 
16 
example, for SC 1A, the Panel’s proposal produces increases ranging from 
17 
0.94 to 1.24 times the 12.97 percent increase for the average customer, and 
18 
the effects are progressive, increasing with increasing usage.  As the rate 
19 
design moves toward inclining rates, customers with either low or high 
20 
usage have increases while customers in the middle have decreases. 
21 
71


--- Page 72 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 70 of 74 
 
 
1 
In addition, for SC 1B, the Panel’s proposal produces increases ranging 
2 
from 0.90 to 1.23 times the 6.92 percent increase for the average customer.  
3 
In this case, the increase in the tail block places an increasing burden on 
4 
higher usage customers, with inclining rates the average customer would 
5 
see a decrease of 16 percent while the higher usage customers would see an 
6 
increase of 46 percent. 
7 
 
8 
Q. 
Please summarize the Panel’s conclusions from this study. 
9 
A. 
The results illustrated by the study – widely divergent percentage increases 
10 
among customer groups within a class, and huge burdens on lower and/or 
11 
higher usage customers – are not acceptable from a ratemaking perspective.  
12 
The Panel notes that if the customer charge were maintained at the present 
13 
level, the effect for both SC 1A and SC 1B would be exacerbated. 
14 
 
15 
The Panel’s proposed rate design includes modest reductions in slope (i.e., 
16 
ratio of tail block to mid-block is increasing).  The Panel supports 
17 
continuing the modest changes it has proposed in this proceeding. 
18

XIV. 
Gas Marginal Cost Study 
8 
Q. 
Please provide an overview of the Gas Marginal Cost Study. 
9 
A. 
The purpose of the MCS, presented in Exhibit ___ (RDP-9), is to compute 
10 
the incremental, or marginal, cost to the utility to provide the next unit of 
11 
service (i.e., the next dekatherm of design-day demand or the next customer 
12 
connected).  The Company is presenting an MCS for distribution demand 
13 
costs only; customer costs and commodity costs are not included.  As shown 
14 
on Exhibit ___ (RDP-9), Schedule 1, the proposed Marginal Delivery Cost 
15 
is $1.01 per dth.  Customers participating in the Company’s Excelsior Jobs 
16 
Program (“EJP”) will pay the marginal delivery cost rate for all gas 
17 
consumption in excess of the consumption included in the applicable 
18 
minimum charge.  Based on the Company’s proposal to move ETIP costs 
19 
into base rates, EJP customers will also be charged an ETIP rate in addition 
20 
to the marginal rate so that they continue to be eligible to participate in 
21 
74


--- Page 75 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 73 of 74 
 
Company-sponsored energy efficiency programs. 
1 
 
2 
Q. 
What are the components of marginal costs in the MCS? 
3 
A. 
The MCS includes the capital cost of the assets needed to serve an additional 
4 
unit of design-day demand, as well as the O&M costs related to the assets. 
5 
 
6 
  
The initial capital cost is developed by quantifying the relationship between 
7 
capital spending for growth, and the growth (additional dekatherms 
8 
delivered) supported.  The initial capital cost is converted to an annual cost, 
9 
representing the amount that would be included in the annual revenue 
10 
requirement to reflect return on rate base plus associated income tax, 
11 
depreciation expense, property tax and insurance. 
12 
 
13 
  
In addition to the annualized capital cost and the associated O&M costs, the 
14 
marginal cost includes property tax and insurance costs related to the assets. 
15 
 
16 
  
Marginal Demand Cost is stated in dollars per delivered dekatherm. 
17 
 
18 
XV. 
Levelized Rate Increases 
19 
Q. 
Does the Company support levelizing the proposed rate increases over 
20 
term of a potential multi-year rate plan? 
21 
75


--- Page 76 ---
Testimony of the Rate Design Panel (KEDLI) 
Page 74 of 74 
 
A.  
Yes. To ease the impact on customer bills, the Company will consider 
1 
options to phase-in the proposed revenue increases over the term of a multi-
2 
year plan. 
3 
 
4 
Q. 
Does this conclude the Panel’s testimony? 
5 
A. 
Yes, it does. 
6

ECOSS Methodology

KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid LI (KEDLI) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The testimony of the Rate Design Panel describes the purpose of performing an Embedded Cost 
of Service Study (“ECOSS”), and summarizes the methodology used to prepare the ECOSS in 
this proceeding.  The testimony describes the three-step ECOSS process (functionalization, 
classification, class allocation) used to analyze each element of the revenue requirement, in order 
to assign or allocate it among the rate classes. 
This Schedule 9 describes the ECOSS methodology in more detail.  Part 1 describes the three-
step ECOSS process. 
Part II describes how each element of the revenue requirement- rate base, expense and revenue- 
was assigned or allocated in each of the three steps.  Plant, expenses and revenues are identified 
using the Uniform System of Accounts (FERC Accounts).  Part II serves as a guide when 
reviewing the other schedules in this exhibit. 
Part 1. DETAILED ECOSS METHODOLOGY 
The purpose of an ECOSS is to apportion fairly a utility’s total revenue requirement, including 
plant and other investments, operating expenses, depreciation, and taxes among the rate classes 
served by the utility.  The ECOSS computes for each rate class the revenue to be collected in 
order to produce the overall required rate of return on rate base.  This information provides 
valuable guidance in revenue allocation, and in the development of rates, to recover the revenue 
requirement from all rate classes. 
The three steps of the ECOSS are: 
Functionalization-  Cost elements are separated among the utility’s basic service 
functions, by determining what physical purpose each cost element serves.  KEDNY’s 
functions are: Gas Supply and Storage; Transmission; Distribution; Metering and Billing; 
Collections; Sales Promotion; and Procurement. 
Classification-  Each functionalized cost elements is classified according as Customer-
related (connects customers to the distribution system); Demand-related (meets design 
day capacity requirements) or Commodity-related (Deliver gas commodity to customers). 
Class Allocation-  Cost elements that have been functionalized and classified are 
allocated among the service classes, using an appropriate allocation factor for each cost 
element.  Allocation factors can be external (e.g., number of customers, deliveries, design 
day requirements sales and historical bad debt experience) or internal (e.g., property 
insurance is based on plant investment). 
264


--- Page 265 ---
Exhibit___ (RDP-3) 
Schedule 9 
Page 2 of 5 
 
KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid LI (KEDLI) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Part 2. ALLOCATOR FOR EACH ELEMENT OF THE REVENUE REQUIREMENT 
A. Rate Base 
1. Intangible Plant (FERC Accounts 301-303) 
Primarily capitalized software costs for new and updated financial and operating 
systems.  Allocated in proportion to plant investment, based on a review of the 
applications that Intangible Plant comprises. 
2. LNG / Storage Plant (FERC Accounts 360-363) 
Assets needed to meet design day and seasonal requirements.  LNG and Storage plant 
are classified as Demand.  Storage is allocated based on seasonal (winter) requirements 
to all customers; LNG is allocated to al firm customers. 
3. Transmission Plant (FERC Accounts 365-368) 
Transmission plant moves natural gas from suppliers to the distribution system, and is 
sized to meet design day requirements.  Classified as Demand and allocated based on 
class design day requirements. 
4. Distribution Plant (FERC Accounts 374-386) 
Mains- Distribution mains connect customers to the distribution system (i.e., customer-
related) and provide capacity to meet design day customer requirements (i.e., demand-
related).  Therefore the cost of mains is classified as partly customer-related and partly 
demand-related.  The minimum size main was determined to be 2 inch plastic, and the 
customer component is estimated to be 46.17%, based on the minimum-system study 
performed.  The customer component was allocated among the classes based on the 
number of customers.  The demand component was allocated among the classes based 
on design-day requirements.  This allocation is discussed in detail in the testimony. 
TC Mains-  Additional costs incurred to connect Temperature Controlled (TC) 
customers were identified.  The portion representing mains extensions was directly 
assigned to the TC classes and allocated among them based on annual usage.  The 
portions of the additional costs representing services and meters were identified as part 
of the analyses for those accounts. 
Measuring & Regulating Equipment- Sized for design day operation, therefore 
classified as demand-related and allocated among the rate classes based on design-day 
requirements.  Industrial equipment is allocated among the non-residential classes. 
265


--- Page 266 ---
Exhibit___ (RDP-3) 
Schedule 9 
Page 3 of 5 
 
KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid LI (KEDLI) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Services- Services connect the customer to the distribution mains.  There is a direct 
correspondence between number of customers and number of services1, therefore 
services are classified as customer-related.  The costs are allocated based on the current 
cost for a typical service line for each rate class. 
Meters- Meters (including installation costs and house regulators) are classified as 
customer-related, and allocated based on the current cost for a typical meter for each 
rate class. 
Land, Structures and Improvements and Other Distribution Plant- Allocated in 
proportion to all other Distribution Plant accounts. 
5. General Plant (FERC Accounts 389-399) 
Primarily Structures & improvements; Tools, shop & garage; and Office furniture and 
equipment.  General plant was functionalized, classified and class allocated in 
proportion to the direct labor content of operating and maintenance expense, because 
these assets primarily support direct labor. 
6. Depreciation Reserve (FERC Accounts 108 and 111) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
7. Other Rate Base Items 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
Materials & Supplies (which includes prepayments) and Cash Working Capital (non-
supply) were allocated in proportion to non-gas O&M costs.  Accumulated Deferred 
Income Tax and CWIP were allocated in proportion to plant in service.  Regulatory 
Assets and Earnings Base Adjustment were allocated in proportion to rate base.  
Storage Gas was allocated based on seasonal (winter) requirements.  Cash Working 
Capital (supply) was allocated in proportion to gas deliveries. 
B. Expenses 
1. Gas Costs (FERC Accounts 804-813)- Allocated in proportion to GAC revenue 
2. LNG / Storage Plant O&M (FERC Accounts 840-849)- Allocated in proportion to 
LNG and / or Storage plant (as described above). 
                                                 
1 This is not a 1:1 correspondence; an adjustment is made for multiple-account premises. 
266


--- Page 267 ---
Exhibit___ (RDP-3) 
Schedule 9 
Page 4 of 5 
 
KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid LI (KEDLI) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
3. Transmission O&M (FERC Accounts 850-867)- Allocated in proportion to 
Transmission plant (classified as Demand and allocated based on class design day 
requirements) 
4. Distribution O&M (FERC Accounts 870-894) 
Mains, Services, Meters, Regulating Equipment- Allocated on the same basis as the 
assets to which they relate. 
Operations Supervision & Engineering and Operations Supervision & Engineering- 
Allocated based on direct labor content of O&M accounts. 
Customer Installations and Other O&M - Allocated based on a special study to identify 
the activities reflected in each account. 
5. Customer Accounts Expenses (FERC Accounts 901-919) 
These accounts were functionalized among Collections, Billing and Distribution based 
on a study of competitive functions performed by the utility.  The accounts are all 
customer-related. 
Supervision (Account 901)-  Allocated in proportion to Customer records and 
collections (Account 903). 
Meter reading (Account 902)-  Allocated based on the investment in meters. 
Customer records and collections (Account 902)-  Billing-related activities are Print 
and mail bills, and Bill calculation.  Collections-related activities are a portion of Call 
center, Credit & collections, Collections and Field Collections.  Distribution-related 
activities are the balance of Call center, Credit & collections, Collections, Field 
Collections and Payment processing as well as Postage outbound and Postage inbound. 
Each functionalized activity was allocated among the rate classes using an appropriate 
allocation factor, and the results were summed to compute allocators for Account 903- 
Distribution, Account 903- Billing and Account 903- Collections. 
Uncollectible accounts expense (Account 904)-  Allocated based on historical write-off 
experience. 
Miscellaneous customer accounts (Account 905)-  Activities are primarily customer 
contact; allocation based on number of customers. 
Customer assistance expenses (Account 908) and Information & instructional (Account 
909)-  Primarily costs for energy efficiency programs; allocated in proportion to 
Energy Efficiency revenue.

--- Page 268 ---
Exhibit___ (RDP-3) 
Schedule 9 
Page 5 of 5 
 
KeySpan Gas East Corporation d/b/a National Grid LI (KEDLI) 
Embedded Cost of Service Study (ECOSS) Methodology 
 
Demonstration & selling ( (Account  912) and Advertising (Account 913)-  Allocated 
based on Gas delivery volumes. 
6. Administrative & General expenses (FERC Accounts 920-939) are grouped as follows: 
 Most A&G expenses are labor-related, and are functionalized, classified and 
allocated in proportion to direct labor content of O&M accounts. 
 Plant-related expenses are functionalized, classified and allocated in proportion 
to according to gross plant. 
 Franchise requirements (Account 927) and Regulatory commission expense 
(Account 928) are functionalized to Distribution, classified as Demand and 
allocated based on Rate base. 
 Miscellaneous General Expenses were allocated based on firm deliveries. 
7. Depreciation and Amortization Expense (FERC Accounts 403-407) 
Each component was allocated in proportion to the corresponding asset cost. 
8. Taxes other than on income 
Property taxes were allocated in proportion to plant, excluding services and meters.  
Payroll taxes were allocated in proportion to direct labor content.  Other taxes were 
allocated in proportion to plant. 
9. Income Taxes 
Income Taxes were allocated in proportion to Pretax income. 
C. Revenue 
Revenue was functionalized and classified based on revenue requirements and 
allocated based on forecast revenue at present rates in the Historic Test Year. 
Rent from gas property was allocated based on design day demand, reflecting the 
assets that give rise to the revenue.  Late payment revenue was allocated based on 
historical write-off experience.  Billing to ESCOs, which is on a per-customer basis, 
was allocated based on number of customers.  Other Revenues were allocated based on 
gas deliveries.  Joint Facilities revenue was allocated based on design day 
requirements.

Notes: 
(a) Balancing OFO MAY be issued. Non-complying customers may also be interrupted for system reliability.
(b) Peaking Supplies may be dispatched when non-firm demand response customers are ON in the following circumstances:
1.If peaking supplies must be dispatched ratably across a weekend and/or holiday with varying temperatures above and below 15°F.
2.Peaking supplies based on a day ahead call option are dispatched based on a forecasted low temperature of 15°F or below. If the actual low temperature 
exceeds the forecasted low temperature, then the non-firm demand response customers may be allowed to burn gas if the system load decreases accordingly.
3.In all cases where non-firm demand response customers are on, LNG and non-ratable peaking will be minimized to preserve winter deliverability.
(c) One or more non-firm demand response customers may be interrupted if needed for gas system reliability.
(d) Depends on distribution system location - may need to interrupt individual customers.
(e) Peaking Supplies to be dispatched based upon a DESIGN rule curve in ALL cases. Least-cost dispatch of LNG will not occur: 
(1) prior to February 15th or 2) if system and/or portfolio reliability is threatened. LNG use for training/testing does not apply.
(f) Balancing OFO WILL be issued. Non-complying customers will be interrupted for system reliability.
(g) Monthly balanced interruptible transportation customers will be interrupted.
(h) Maximum of FOUR hours of LNG sendout. LNG sendout for plant idling/cool down does not apply.
(i)Non-Firm Demand Response Tier 2 Sales Customers will be interrupted as described above as soon as practical.
(j) Interruptible Power Plants operating on KEDNY SC 14 and SC18 and KEDLI SC7 and SC14 may have contractual limits on the number of days of allowed interruptibility.
(k) Note that the 15 °F temperature is illustrative. The applicable Designated Interruption Temperature is set each year. Tier 1 customers in KEDNY will be interrupted
when the Company receives a report that the LAGUARDIA AIRPORT TEMPERATURE has reached the Designated Interruption Temperature. Tier 1 customers in KEDLI 
will be interrupted when the Company receives a report that the FARMINGDALE AIRPORT TEMPERATURE has reached the Designated Interruption Temperature.
(l) Note that the 20 °F temperature is illustrative. The applicable Designated Interruption Temperature is set each year. Tier 2 customers in KEDNY will be interrupted
when the Company receives a report that the LAGUARDIA AIRPORT TEMPERATURE has reached the Designated Interruption Temperature. Tier 2 customers in KEDLI 
will be interrupted when the Company receives a report that the FARMINGDALE AIRPORT TEMPERATURE has reached the Designated Interruption Temperature.

Resume of Howard S. Gorman 
 
Page 1 
SUMMARY 
Mr. Gorman has more than 30 years of experience in the energy industry, including 20 
years in rate and regulatory proceedings.  His areas of expertise include embedded class cost of 
service studies, marginal cost studies, revenue allocation, rate design and revenue requirements, 
for both electric and gas utilities.  He has testified as an expert witness before the Massachusetts 
Department of Public Utilities, New Jersey Board of Public Utilities, New Hampshire Public 
Utilities Commission, New York State Public Service Commission, Ontario Energy Board, 
Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission and Rhode Island Public Utilities Commission.  Mr. 
Gorman also has experience in financial modeling, financial analysis and forecasting, developing 
accounting systems, and treasury and financial management. 
PROFESSIONAL EMPLOYMENT 
• 2010 - Present  
HSG Group, Inc. 
▪ President 
• 1997 - 2010 
 
Black & Veatch Corporation (R.J. Rudden Associates, Inc. before 
2005) 
▪ Principal Consultant 
• 1995 - 1997 
 
Independent Consultant 
• 1987 – 1995   
Trigen Energy Corporation 
▪ 1987-1993 Corporate Controller; Trigen was formed in 1987 
▪ 1993-1995 Treasurer; Trigen had IPO with NYSE listing in 1994 
• 1982 - 1987 
 
Coleco Industries, Inc. 
▪ Director, Treasury 
• 1976 - 1979 
 
Touche Ross & Co. 
▪ Staff Accountant 
PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE 
Utility Accounting and Costing 
Mr. Gorman has performed numerous class cost of service studies for electric and gas 
utilities, and has also developed and supported revenue requirements, revenue allocation proposals 
and rate designs.  These assignments included development of test year data, establishment of cost 
causality, selection of allocation bases, development of allocators, and analysis of customer 
impacts and policy considerations. 
Energy Project Analysis 
Mr. Gorman has performed financial analyses of energy-related assets, including electric 
and gas distribution companies, power plants and transmission operators.  These analyses included 
development of cash flows and financial statements based on both regulatory and accounting

Energy Project Financing 
Mr. Gorman has negotiated and completed transactions including construction and term 
loans, tax-exempt bonds, taxable bonds, subordinated debt and asset-backed (receivables and 
inventory) revolving credit facilities.  He has worked successfully with lenders and borrowers to 
source and structure transactions and was instrumental in negotiating loan documents and in 
designing power sale and supply procurement contracts to be financed. 
Accounting and Financial Management 
Mr. Gorman has extensive experience in financial accounting.  As controller of Trigen 
Energy Corporation, he founded and built the finance and accounting function; developed reports, 
procedures and management tools; and managed subsidiary controllers across North America, 
including an IPO with NYSE listing.  He managed the corporate insurance portfolios and the 
benefit plans for Trigen Energy Corporation and for Coleco Industries and has bought and sold 
interest rate and currency forward contracts for the purpose of managing risk. 
Modeling and Decision Support 
Mr. Gorman is an accomplished modeler with expertise in spreadsheet applications.  He 
has developed analytical tools for valuations, projections and simulations.  These models have 
been applied to financial analysis, cost allocations, rate design and pricing, forecasting revenue 
requirements, and tax and accounting matters.  Several of these models have contained interactive 
modules for automated scenario testing and sensitivity analysis.

Professional Experience  
Manager, NY Gas Pricing, December 2015 – Present  
I am responsible for the supervision of the study, analysis and design of retail gas delivery service rates 
and terms and conditions for gas service, including testifying and supporting such rates and tariffs 
before the NYPSC for National Grid USA’s three New York State gas utilities – KEDNY, KEDLI and 
Niagara Mohawk. The gas pricing department is also responsible for providing customer service and 
billing support, negotiated contract support, and guidance in the interpretation and application of retail 
gas delivery service tariffs.  
Senior/Lead Pricing Analyst, NY Electric Pricing-National Grid, Jan 2006 – Dec 2015  
My responsibilities as lead analyst included analytical support for electric standby service including cost 
and regulatory analysis, deferral accounting process design, rate design, and discovery responses.  I also 
had responsibility for the development of various surcharge factors including the monthly and annual 
reconciliations for the Company’s electric commodity reconciliations and merchant function charges.  I 
was also the regulatory lead for several new initiatives including the development of residential time of 
use rates and the implementation of the NYPA residential agricultural discount program.  
Senior Financial Analyst, Planning and Financial Analysis- National Grid Feb 2000 – Jan 2006  
My responsibilities as senior analyst included the preparation of margin reports monthly for internal 
management review, the evaluation of margin variances, the preparation of monthly revenue analysis and 
development of the annual budget for margin related items.  
Financial Analyst, Planning and Financial Analysis- Felix Schoeller Technical Papers Sept 1998 – Feb 
2000  
My responsibilities as senior analyst included supervision of the daily activities of the general accounting 
staff including A/P, A/R and general ledger transactions, the coordination of the month end closing 
process, the review of all journal entries, and the preparation of various monthly reports including balance 
sheet analysis and monthly departmental budget vs actual analysis.  
Supervisor of Fixed Assets, The Penn Traffic Company  Oct 1996 - Sept 1998  
My responsibilities as the supervisor of the fixed assets department included the supervision of the daily 
activities of accounting staff including the payment of invoices for capital projects, addition of assets to 
the system, and weekly and monthly reporting.  In addition, I was responsible for tracking all capital 
project spending for new stores, store remodels, and major equipment purchases for all divisions of Penn 
Traffic and verification that capital budgets were met, and the preparation of monthly book and yearly tax 
depreciation reports along with the preparation of personal property tax returns.
